One muon through the whole simulation chain

A cosmic muon crosses the 30 mm drift gap. Each stage of the chain is a separate code, and the list on the right says which one and how far it is trusted. At the end, the simulated peak-strip pulse is laid over the real average det3 pulse at the same angle. Switch the ion signal off to see what the data look like. Only Geant4 simulates this muon from first principles: the later stages draw random numbers from tables that Magboltz and Garfield++ computed once beforehand (what runs per event).

    What runs per event, and what ran once

    Garfield never sees this muon

    The Geant4 primary electrons are not handed to Garfield++/Magboltz to drift and avalanche. Garfield and Magboltz ran beforehand on single electrons, once per gas and HV point, and measured a handful of numbers. Each event then moves every primary electron on its own, but by drawing random numbers from those results. Alexandra's P2_Geant_Garfield works the same way (her Stage B is thinner: transparency fixed at 1, gain and induction still placeholders).

    Ran once, offlineper gas / HV point · hours on condor or the desktop

    • Magboltz gas table → drift speed vd, diffusion σT, σL vs E design/gas/
    • Garfield++ S2: single electrons through the woven-mesh field map → transparency ε response/meshcell/
    • Garfield++ S3 microscopic avalanches, 10³–10⁴ seed electrons per point → Polya ḡ, θ, landing spread σ₀, ion fraction f and transit response/avalanche/ → aval_calib.json
    • S1/W2 solver + COMSOL: time-dependent weighting potentials of the resistive strips → current kernels response/solver/
    • DREAM shaper model; noise measured from data

    Every eventGeant4 run + response/digitizer/digitize.py · fast

    1. Geant4 tracks the muon → clusters, each with nPrimary electrons (W and Fano already applied)
    2. each electron: drift time z/vd, plus Gaussian σL, σT smearing
    3. survives the mesh with probability ε (one coin flip)
    4. gain drawn from Polya(ḡ, θ), landing smeared by σ₀ ≈ 33 µm
    5. charge × kernel lookup → current on each nearby strip, with the ion tail
    6. DREAM shaper → 60 ns samples + noise → the same wft reconstruction as data

    Why not Garfield per event

    Microscopic tracking follows every collision of every electron. A muon leaves ~270 primaries in 30 mm, and each one becomes ~24 000 electrons in the gap: ~6 million avalanche electrons per event, plus up to 30 mm of drift each. One S3 gain bracket of single electrons alone took 42 CPU-hours. Thousands of events that way is not feasible.

    What it assumes

    Electrons in one event don't affect each other (no space charge or charging-up within an event), so each one can be sampled independently from single-electron statistics. That is the standard approach for MPGDs at these rates. Electrons are moved one by one, not as a packet per cluster, because diffusion (826 µm) is what sets the strip sharing.

    What we lose

    Correlations and shapes the simple model drops: ε and the gain don't depend on where the electron hits the mesh cell, and diffusion is Gaussian. Any error in an offline number goes into every event. Example: ε = 0.955 is a Garfield stepping artefact; with null-collision steps the 56-slice campaign gives 0.993, but its gain per surviving electron is 3 % lower, so the charge reaching the strips moves only +0.7 % (2026-10-16).

    Physics in the page: the independent toy model (MX17_Geant/scratchpad/2026-10-12/toy_pulse.py): Magboltz v = 39.1 µm/ns and diffusion, 91 e⁻/cm in 3.8-e⁻ clusters, mesh transparency 0.955, parallel-plate ion current (f = 0.91, T = 340 ns, Ar⁺), DREAM PZC + Sallen-Key shaper at 180 ns. The resistive spreading is drawn but not computed. Real and chain averages: peak strip, unsaturated, no quality cut, aligned at the leading 50 %.
